extracted.intended_audience: law students and practitioners of United States patent law (judges, litigators, scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of substantive principles governing patent infringement, who may sue, and which courts/venues have jurisdiction in U.S. patent cases; includes rules on venue, service, parties, and remedies (including suits against the U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility alone not determinative of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility of the plaintiff's and the defendant's process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, is not alone a criterion of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative utility must be considered together with comparative character; mere diminished utility of a defendant's device does not excuse infringement nor does greater utility of defendant avoid infringement if it results from an addition to the patented thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements/additions do not avoid infringement if added to patented thing
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's machine may be better than that covered by the patent and may be an improvement; if that superiority resulted from some addition to the latter, it will have no tendency to avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It matters not that the addition or improvement is patentable or patented; superiority due to added features that are built on the patented invention will not avoid infringement (see citations e.g., Pitts v. Wemple; Benjamin Electric Mfg. Co. v. Dale Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different mode of construction/operation may avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant has discovered an entirely different mode of construction and operation, in that event it does not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with mere additions to the same basic invention; where the defendant's device is of a different species (entirely different mode), it may avoid infringement even if it performs similar functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species vs genus patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's machine may be of a different species and of course cannot infringe a patent of a different species than itself although it might infringe the genus patent of which both are species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the accused device falls within the claims (genus) or is a different species; species-patent vs genus-patent distinctions determine possible infringement relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative utility relevant only with comparative character
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative utility is relevant to questions of infringement when its consideration is coupled with the consideration of comparative character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention never useful enough to be used in any productive business cannot be made to prevent the progress of a useful art by being asserted against a succeeding, successful invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: An unsuccessful invention cannot suppress a successful one
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention which was never useful enough to be used in any productive business cannot be used to prevent progress toward successful inventions; an invention which failed cannot be used to suppress a succeeding invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not allow a failed invention to chill technological progress by blocking successful inventions that lie along the road to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge/intent not required for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute an infringement of a patent, it is not necessary that the infringer should have known of the existence of the patent at the time he infringed it; nor is it necessary that he should have known his doings to constitute an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is strict in this sense: independent invention or lack of knowledge of the patent does not avert liability (cases cited: Parker v. Haworth; United States v. Berdan Fire Arms Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent creation does not avert infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is not averted by the fact that the infringer contrived his own process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter without any knowledge of the patent infringed thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law treats unauthorized practice of the claimed invention as infringement even if independently developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts (district courts) have original jurisdiction over patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The District Courts of the United States have original jurisdiction of all suits at law or in equity arising under the patent laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This jurisdiction is independent of State statutes; the Judicial Code vested this jurisdiction in federal district courts (historical statutory citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts have no jurisdiction over patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts have no jurisdiction of actions for infringements of patents (cases and Supreme Court holdings confirm this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although earlier statutes and debates existed, the law is established that such cases are exclusively cognizable in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract actions between private parties relevant to patents are not patent-law actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions brought to enforce contracts between private parties, relevant to patent rights, are not actions arising under the patent laws of the United States and therefore are not cognizable as such in United States courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are exceptions and nuanced decisions (e.g., New Marshall Engine Co. v. Marshall Engine Co.) where the specifics may pull a case into or out of federal jurisdiction; one must analyze whether the bill requires construction/validity determinations of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hartell v. Tilghman principle (license defense can affect jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a complainant states a patent right and its use, and alleges the defendant's justification is an alleged license (and avers no such license exists), and the defendant admits the patent and use and defends only on the license, the action may not be one arising under the patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine is limited and should not be extended beyond its factual elements; courts will not allow defendants to defeat jurisdiction by artful pleadings in multiple forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff suing as a 'naked infringer' invokes federal jurisdiction despite defendant's defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a plaintiff decides to sue a defendant as a naked infringer, the Federal courts have jurisdiction, and such jurisdiction cannot be ousted by any answer which the defendant may interpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff's complaint asserts infringement (and not merely contract/license issues), federal jurisdiction remains even if defendant later pleads license or other defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue: suits must be brought where defendant inhabits or where infringement and regular place of business occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Suits for infringement must be brought in the district of which the defendant is an inhabitant, or in any district in which the defendant has committed acts of infringement and has a regular and established place of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory restrictions (e.g., Act of March 3, 1897, re-enacted 1911) limit venue; these are personal privileges that can be waived by general appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: General appearance waives venue defenses but is limited by scope of original action
rubrics_metrics.description: General appearance is a waiver of the venue privilege, but it is limited in application by the scope of the action in which the appearance is filed and does not warrant allowing an amendment that sets up a new, different or distinct cause of action not originally within jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appearance cannot retroactively confer jurisdiction for a cause of action that the court could not have entertained at the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple defendants in different districts of same State: patent suits governed by special rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision allowing suit where two or more defendants reside in different federal districts of the same State (with duplicate subpoenas) does not apply to suits for infringement of patents; each defendant must be within the scope of the older Act (March 3, 1807) requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent venue rules are stricter than ordinary joinder provisions; treat each defendant's residence/place-of-business jurisdictionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and established place of business — existence required at time suit begun
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the jurisdiction is not based on habitation, the existence of a regular and established place of business in the district, at the time the suit is begun, is necessary to the jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact of an established place of business must be proven if denied; temporary exhibits (e.g., exposition booths) are not regular places of business; examples and cases illustrate nuances (selling corporation's place may be regular for manufacturer; mere solicitation agents may not create such place).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibitor space is not a 'regular and established place of business'
rubrics_metrics.description: A space occupied by an exhibitor in an exposition for the purpose of showing articles to the public is not a regular and established place of business within the meaning of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish temporary exhibition activities from established business locations when assessing venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary solicitation agency may or may not create regular place of business
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturing corporation maintaining an agency for preliminary negotiation of sales has a regular and established place of business; but if the preliminary negotiation is not followed by any sale or subsequent use of an infringing article in the district, the district court has no jurisdiction on account of that agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preliminary negotiation is followed by a sale outside the district for subsequent use inside the district, jurisdiction may exist because the manufacturer contributed to infringing use in the district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traveling sales representative who merely solicits orders often does not create venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a manufacturing company employs a representative who merely solicits orders and forwards them to the home office for execution, the representative's activities do not constitute a regular and established place of business in the district (W. S. Tyler Co. v. Ludlow-Saylor Wire Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include salary/commissions, where sale is consummated, whether representative shares office expenses or is employed by other entities; these determine venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service on agents at regular place of business is permissive; corporation may be served if found within district
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the suit is brought in a district where the defendant has a 'regular and established place of business' service of process 'may be made by service upon the agent or agents engaged in conducting such business' is permissive only; where the defendant is found within the district service may be made on the corporation itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service by agent is an allowable method but not mandatory; actual presence of corporation in district is sufficient for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to prove jurisdictional facts when denied
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary general appearance by the defendant does not relieve the plaintiff from proving the jurisdictional facts if the allegations concerning them are denied; if infringement in the district is denied, the plaintiff must take evidence to prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If jurisdictional facts are disputed, they are to be tried on evidence; defendant may move to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction after plaintiff's evidence in chief if plaintiff fails to prove infringement in the district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement for non-resident: must be actual, not merely threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of jurisdiction over a non-resident the infringement must be actual and not merely threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of threatened acts alone are insufficient to establish venue for non-residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division-level venue rule: bring suit in division where defendant resides
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a district contains more than one division, every action for infringement brought in that district on the ground of the habitation of the defendant must be brought in the division where he resides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple defendants reside in different divisions, suit must be brought in the proper division for one of them consistent with statutory rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Claims has jurisdiction for suits against U.S. for government use of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Claims is the tribunal with jurisdiction of actions brought by owners of patent rights against the government of the United States for compensation for the use by the Government of patents and patent rights owned by individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such suits are subject to a six-year statute of limitations; absent an established royalty the claimant may recover what a reasonable royalty for an express license would have been (Act of June 25, 1910, 36 Stat. 851).

rubrics_metrics.name: United States sovereign immunity limited by statute (Act of June 25, 1910)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States cannot be sued except where it has consented by statute; the Act of June 25, 1910 gave the Court of Claims jurisdiction for recovery of reasonable compensation for Government use of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to the Act remedies vs the Government were limited; after the Act claimants may seek compensation in Court of Claims; suits against individual officers for unauthorized use are no longer viable in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of government officers for unauthorized use is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no longer the law that an action will lie against agents of the Government for unauthorized making, using, or selling of patented things for the Government; remedy is via Court of Claims statutory jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Section 157 and cases regarding personal liability of officers; the statutory remedy supplants direct suits against officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be plaintiff in patent actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff or complainant in an action based on infringement may be the patentee, the sole assignee of that patent, or any grantee under a patent may sue alone for infringement committed within his territory; an owner of equitable title may sue in equity if the defendant is the patentee or his assignee; partnerships may sue in the partnership name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory and case law (Revised Statutes §4919 and authorities) define who has standing to sue; forms of ownership and timing of interest (see next item) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of ownership for actions at law vs equity
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action at law it is enough if the plaintiff was the patentee, assignee, or grantee of the rights infringed at the time the infringement sued upon was committed; in equity, which seeks injunctions, the plaintiff generally must have a present interest to obtain an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief (injunction) generally requires present ownership/interest; assignation or change in ownership may affect available remedies though jurisdiction will not lapse if assignor owned patent when filing for injunction/money recovery and later assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment after filing does not generally defeat equitable jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a complainant owns a patent infringed when he files his bill for an injunction and a money recovery, jurisdiction will not lapse when he assigns the future of his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may retain jurisdiction despite subsequent assignment of rights, depending on circumstances (doctrine and cases cited).
